questions.question: In fac 0 = 1, which word names 0, and which names the whole line?
options: 0 is the expression; the whole line is a pattern
0 is a pattern; the whole line is an equation
0 is an equation; the whole line is an expression
0 is a funcName; the whole line is a pattern
questions.explanation: 0 is what fac's argument is matched against — a pattern. fac 0 = 1 in full — name, pattern, and the result it produces — is one equation. A function is the complete set of its equations.
optionFeedback: 0 is not an expression here; it is the pattern being matched against. 1, on the right of =, is the expression.
Correct — 0 is a literal pattern, and fac 0 = 1 taken as a whole is one equation.
An equation is the whole funcName-pattern-equals-expression line, not a single value inside it — 0 alone is too small to be called an equation.
funcName refers to the function's own name, fac, not to the pattern being matched inside one of its equations.

questions.question: Why does reversing the two equations of square make square 0 return 0 instead of 1?
options: Because Haskell always uses the last matching equation, not the first
Because the first equation, square y = y * y, has a variable pattern that matches every possible argument including 0, so it is used before GHC ever reaches the literal-0 equation below it
Because 0 * 0 and 1 happen to be mathematically equivalent in this context
Because GHC refuses to compile the reversed version, so the old behaviour persists
questions.explanation: Pattern matching tries equations strictly top to bottom and commits to the first one that matches. A bare variable pattern like y matches literally any value, 0 included. Once it is first, it intercepts every call — including square 0 — before the more specific square 0 = 1 equation is ever consulted.
optionFeedback: Haskell uses the first matching equation, not the last — that is precisely why ordering (most specific first) matters so much.
0 * 0 is 0, and 1 is 1 — they are not equal; the function genuinely computes the wrong answer once the general pattern shadows the specific one.
The reversed version compiles successfully (with a redundancy warning); it is not rejected, which is exactly why this mistake is dangerous — it fails silently rather than loudly.

questions.question: What general rule does the square example establish for ordering pattern-matching equations?
options: Equations should be ordered alphabetically by pattern

The most specific patterns (literals, particular structures) should come before more general patterns (bare variables, wildcards), because a general pattern placed earlier will always intercept the cases meant for the specific ones
It does not matter what order equations are written in, as long as all cases are covered somewhere
Variable patterns should always come first because they are the simplest to read
questions.explanation: Because Haskell commits to the first matching equation, any pattern that matches a strict superset of another pattern's cases must be placed after the more specific one, or it will always win first. This is the same most-specific-first discipline used for guards and conditionals elsewhere in this chapter.
optionFeedback: Pattern ordering has nothing to do with alphabetical sorting of the pattern text.
Order matters a great deal, as the square example demonstrates directly — coverage of all cases is necessary but not sufficient if the order is wrong.
Placing the most general pattern first is exactly the mistake this section warns against — it silently shadows every specific case below it.

questions.question: A lab file compiles cleanly with -Wincomplete-patterns turned on, printing a warning about dayName's missing cases. The student runs dayName 3 anyway. What happens?
options: GHC already rejected the file, so it never runs
The program still throws Non-exhaustive patterns in function dayName at run time — the flag only printed a warning at compile time, it did not add a missing case or prevent the crash
GHC automatically inserts a default case using the warning's information
dayName 3 returns an empty string instead of crashing, because the warning suppresses the exception
questions.explanation: -Wincomplete-patterns is purely diagnostic: it prints a warning at compile time so a human can see the gap and fix it. It changes nothing about how the compiled function behaves. If the programmer ignores the warning and the missing case is actually reached at run time, the exact same Non-exhaustive patterns crash still happens.
optionFeedback: A warning does not stop compilation — the module compiles successfully and dayName remains fully callable; only errors block compilation.
GHC never writes code on your behalf; the warning only reports the gap in the source text you already wrote. Adding the missing case is still the programmer's job.
Nothing about the warning changes dayName's run-time behaviour — the crash is identical whether or not the flag was enabled.

questions.question: What is the actual purpose of turning on -Wincomplete-patterns, given that it cannot prevent a run-time crash on its own?
options: It has no real purpose; it is only there for cosmetic compiler output
It surfaces missing cases early, while you are reading compiler output during development, so you can add the catch-all case yourself before a user's input ever reaches the gap
It automatically fixes non-exhaustive pattern matches
It replaces the need for writing test cases with invalid inputs
questions.explanation: The value of the warning is entirely about timing and visibility: it turns a silent gap in your equations into a message you see immediately after loading the file, rather than a surprise crash discovered later (possibly by an end user). It is a detection tool, not a repair tool or a substitute for exhaustiveness testing.
optionFeedback: It has real diagnostic value — it is exactly how you would discover dayName's gap in this example without manually re-reading every equation.
It never edits your source code; you still have to write the catch-all equation yourself.
Testing invalid or boundary inputs (as this course's six-part process recommends) is still necessary — the warning only helps you catch omissions in the source text, not confirm correctness.

questions.question: In axisOf, why must axisOf (0, 0) = "origin" be listed before axisOf (0, _) = "on the y-axis"?
options: Because tuple patterns must always be listed in the order the components were declared in the type signature
Because (0, 0) also matches the more general pattern (0, _) — if the general one came first, it would intercept every call to axisOf (0, 0) before the specific equation was ever tried
Because Haskell requires a literal-tuple pattern to appear before any pattern containing a wildcard, as a fixed syntax rule
It doesn't actually matter for this function; both orderings produce identical results
questions.explanation: This is the exact same most-specific-first discipline as square 0 versus square y in Section 2, applied to a tuple pattern instead of a plain literal. (0, 0) matches both (0, 0) and (0, _), so whichever is listed first wins for that input — the specific case must come first or it is permanently shadowed.
optionFeedback: Pattern ordering is a matching-order rule, not a rule about mirroring the signature's component order — nothing about (Int, Int) forces this particular sequence.
Correct — this is the tuple-pattern version of the exact ordering rule established for square 0 / square y earlier in this lesson.
There is no such blanket syntax rule; the ordering here follows from what each pattern matches, not from the presence of a wildcard as such.
Reversing the two equations changes the answer for axisOf (0, 0) specifically — swap them and it would print "on the y-axis" instead of "origin".

questions.question: What does axisOf (0, 5) return, and which equation supplies it?
options: "origin", from the first equation, because the first component is 0
"on the y-axis", from the second equation axisOf (0, _) = "on the y-axis", because (0,0) fails to match but (0,_) does
"on the x-axis", from the third equation
"off both axes", from the fourth equation, since neither component is exactly 0 and 0
questions.explanation: (0, 5) does not match the literal pattern (0, 0) — 5 is not 0 — so matching moves to the next equation, (0, _), which matches any tuple with a first component of 0. That equation fires and returns "on the y-axis".
optionFeedback: The first equation requires the second component to be exactly 0 as well; (0, 5) fails that literal match and falls through to the next equation.
Correct — the first equation's literal 0 in the second position fails to match 5, so the second equation, with its wildcard, takes over.
The third equation, (_, 0), requires the second component to be 0 — it is 5 here, so this equation is never reached for this input.
The fourth equation is only reached when none of the first three match; (0, _) already matches (0, 5), so matching stops there.

questions.question: stW is called as stW "boat" (four characters). Why does it return False rather than True?
options: Because 'b' is not the first character of "boat"
Because the pattern ['b', _, _] only matches lists of exactly three elements, and "boat" has four, so the first equation's pattern fails to match regardless of what the characters are
Because stW only works on words, not on arbitrary character lists
Because uppercase and lowercase b are treated differently
questions.explanation: A list pattern like ['b', _, _] encodes both a length requirement (exactly 3) and per-position requirements (first element is 'b', the rest are anything). "boat" has 4 characters, so its length alone fails to match a 3-element pattern — the second equation, stW _, catches it and returns False.
optionFeedback: 'b' is in fact the first character of "boat" — the mismatch is about length, not the first character.
stW works on any [Char] (any character list); nothing about it is specific to English words.
The literal pattern used is 'b' (lowercase); case sensitivity is not what causes this particular result — length is.

questions.question: Why must tail (_:xs) = xs be written with parentheses around _:xs, rather than tail _:xs = xs?
options: Parentheses are purely a style preference recommended by this course
Function application binds more tightly than the : operator, so tail _:xs = xs would parse as (tail _):xs = xs — a completely different, invalid pattern
Without parentheses, GHC would interpret _:xs as a tuple
Parentheses are required around every pattern in Haskell, with no exceptions
questions.explanation: Haskell parses tail _:xs = xs by applying the usual precedence rules: function application (tail _) binds tighter than the infix : operator. So without parentheses the whole left-hand side is read as (tail _) : xs — nonsensical as a function definition. Parenthesising the cons pattern forces _:xs to be read as one single pattern argument to tail.
optionFeedback: This is not a stylistic recommendation — omitting the parentheses changes what the line means and typically produces a compile error, not just an ugly one.
: builds a list (cons), not a tuple; tuples use commas inside parentheses instead.

Plenty of patterns in this lesson are unparenthesised, such as literal patterns like 0 or variable patterns like n — parentheses are specifically needed here because of the : operator's interaction with function-application precedence.
